Why it matters: Huang was a singular leader in the global economy, capable of exciting or calming markets with a single sentence and viewed as a virtually indestructible force behind Nvidia's rise. The big picture: His sudden exit after reports of multiple affairs — one with a suspected Chinese spy and the other with a direct report — has wiped out more than $600 billion in value from Nvidia's market cap. articles.summary: Reed’s view Jensen Huang made a lot of mistakes, but the one that really brought him down was getting too involved in DC. The skillset of a great technologist is the opposite of someone who’s great at politics. Technologists have to think years, sometimes decades in advance. When they figure out a winning formula, they bet everything on it. That’s a really bad way to operate in Washington, where things move on two-year election cycles and commitment to any one idea, faction, or ideology is a liability if and when the political winds change. When Donald Trump was elected president for a second term, it seemed like the world was suddenly a fundamentally different place. The White House was open for business in a way never seen in history. articles.summary: The News Republican and Democratic leaders are coalescing behind a new crackdown on advanced chip exports to China following the Nvidia scandal that could become law by the end of the year. In the House, both Speaker Mike Johnson and Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries favor strengthening chip export controls following revelations that Nvidia’s now former CEO, Jensen Huang, had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy. That’s raised national security concerns about the gargantuan chip manufacturer, which sold $4 billion in chips to Singapore company Megaspeed, which is suspected of diverting that technology to China and under investigation by the Justice Department. Senate Majority Leader John Thune told Semafor that there’s a “high probability” that Congress imposes more restrictions on chip exports to China.
